sources.title: Rodolfo Fattovich: Reconsidering Yeha, circa 800 to 400 BCE, 2009/2010
sources.note: Direct complete author-posted research article, African Archaeological Review 26, 275 to 290. Regional cultural diversity, uncertain territorial/state reconstruction and pottery assemblages. Imported Damot attribution is an inference from BCE dates and decoded northern geometry; not proof of a living Dʿmt monarchy in 300 to 200 BCE.

sources.title: German Archaeological Institute: Archaeological Research in Yeha
sources.note: Direct institutional research project account: settlement from late second millennium BCE, temple seventh century BCE, palace about 800 BCE, collective shaft burials possibly family groups and subsequent Christian reuse. No exact number of palace storeys treated as established.

sources.title: German Archaeological Institute: Yeha project results, landscape and building materials
sources.note: Direct project results tab read at same project ID, not charged as a separate source from overview. Naturraum section: small water systems, rock-cut seasonal storage basin, volcanic rubble, local sandstone and limestone transported about 90 km from Wuqro. Terrace chronology explicitly unresolved and not used.

sources.title: German Archaeological Institute: Antike Wolkenkratzer in Äthiopien?, 9 September 2026
sources.note: Direct dated original project report on Grat Beʿal Gibri structural modelling. Timber/masonry walls established; numerical capacity allowing many storeys is hypothetical and must not be presented as the actual building height. Geometry and floors remain to be incorporated in modelling.

sources.title: Silvia Polla and colleagues: Ceramic and Food Consumption in Ancient Northern Ethiopia, 2024
sources.note: Direct original research abstract and indexed PDF introduction checked; full PDF direct fetch failed. JoGA 2024, 132 to 157, DOI 10.34780/6bno-0fcb. Analysis of absorbed residues and vessel contents, plant/animal fats, fruit-fermentation markers, tentative moringa seed oil. No specific fruit species, drink recipe or whole-population diet inferred.

sources.title: Norbert Nebes: A Woman’s Altar Dedication from Ṣ́ǝrḥan, 2023/2024
sources.note: Direct complete original inscription edition, Aethiopica 26, 16 to 29, published 7 May 2024. Printed 17 line 4 bn / bn and printed 18 translation; printed 21 commentary means son of the son, ancestral generation. Female dedicant and local orthography discussed printed 18 and 22. Author studied a surviving thumbnail; original documentation lost in conflict, no in-situ autopsy. Sample modern Unicode normalization is derived from scholarly reading, not claimed visually checked facsimile.

sources.title: Unicode Consortium: Old South Arabian character chart
sources.note: Official chart directly read. U+10A68 BETH and U+10A6C NUN support normalized display of attested bn bn. The inscription has reversed N in this word; normalized font deliberately does not imitate that palaeographic detail.

sources.title: Sarah Japp: Archaeological Investigations on the Church Forecourt of Yeha, 2019
sources.note: Direct original excavation abstract, 2013 to 2018 sondage. Earliest settlement late second millennium BCE, Ethio-Sabaean layers first half of first millennium BCE, hiatus in this trench during second half, later Aksumite reoccupation. Local stratigraphy is not treated as proof of total regional depopulation.

sources.title: Daniel Foliard: Rabah Fadlallah (Sciences Po, 2012)
sources.note: Research-network biography, paragraphs 1 to 3. Its simplified early chronology is not used for an exact founding year. Public copy identifies enslavement and regional destruction without repeating colonial stereotypes.

sources.title: Kyari Mohammed: Borno under Rabih Fadl Allah, 1893 to 1900 (1997)
sources.note: Original research using administrative records, oral interviews and earlier accounts. Printed pp. 281 to 299. Public claims concern the Borno phase, not the eastern imported polygon.

sources.title: Émile Gentil: La chute de l’empire de Rabah, chapter VIII (1902)
sources.note: Primary account by a French colonial conqueror, describing his June 1900 journey and visit after Rabih’s death. Use only attributed observations; reject racial hierarchy, hostile moral generalizations and hearsay household totals. Chapter VIII, opening journey and Dikwa palace/market descriptions.

sources.title: John E. Lavers: The Awlad Rabih, 22 April 1900 to 23 August 1901 (1994)
sources.note: Original Paideuma 40 article, pp. 215 to 242, full primary research text indexed through a scan mirror. Originally a 1975 seminar paper, published without updating. Introduction distinguishes the 1879 to 1891 Central African campaigns from 1893 Borno conquest; subsequent narrative follows surviving family and followers.

sources.title: Xavier Luffin: Un autre regard sur l’histoire congolaise: les documents arabes et swahilis dans les archives belges, 1880 to 1899 (2020)
sources.note: Royal Academy for Overseas Sciences critical document edition. MRAC.STRO.1, printed pp. 335 to 337 (human PDF pages 335 to 337), dated 28 November 1894. Arabic diplomatic letter of al-Sanusi al-Bakr, not Rabih’s autograph. Arabic text and French translation directly read. Same volume also supplies a separately identified Mirambo-era document; combined volume budget must remain under 200 words.

sources.title: Marek Pawełczak: From marginality to expansion: three polities on the East African central caravan route (2024)
sources.note: Original research article in Studies in African Languages and Cultures 58, printed pp. 39 onward (human PDF page 37 onward). Comparative polities are Mirambo, Nyungu and Mkwawa, not this imported label’s exact trio. Unyanyembe remains distinct. Printed pp. 52 to 54 for local chiefs, governors and supply obligations.

sources.title: Aylward Shorter: Nyungu-ya-Mawe and the Empire of the Ruga-rugas (1968)
sources.note: Original Journal of African History research article. Publisher’s full extract directly read, independently same extract at African Union library. Both leaders died 1884; Nyungu’s polity survived until German dismantling in 1895. Avoid its outdated claim that this was the only realistic unification.

sources.title: Philip Gooding and colleagues: Resilience and vulnerability to drought in Unyanyembe (2023)
sources.note: Original climate-history research, full text directly read. Sections on droughts of the 1830s and 1870s to 1890s, especially crop choices, war/stockades/tsetse, Mirambo’s 1884 collapse, Unyanyembe from 1893. Drought is a contributing factor, not a complete single-cause explanation.

sources.title: Karin Pallaver: Tanzania in the nineteenth century: Muslim communities, long-distance trade and wage labour (2012)
sources.note: Original historical research based partly on White Fathers archives; full article read. Sections on caravan professions, wages, cloth/beads, and gradual incorporation of coastal healing/religious practices. Public copy says many porters were wage workers, not that every porter was free.

sources.title: Stephen J. Rockel: Caravan porters of the Nyika (University of Toronto, 1997)
sources.note: Original doctoral research, printed pp. 100 to 101 on household labour and crafts, fully indexed institutional PDF passage read; direct PDF fetch failed. Author explicitly cautions that Grant’s account does not always distinguish free women from enslaved women. No universal gender rule inferred.

proposedOverrides.name: Mirambo, Unyanyembe and Ukimbu
proposedOverrides.summary: Separate western Tanzanian powers linked by trade, rivalry and changing alliances.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Ancient northern location and BCE dates indicate intended Dʿmt, not medieval Damot farther south. Both chronological and territorial precision remain unsupported. Public name/opening identify contextual coverage rather than asserting the kingdom lasted to 200 BCE. Earlier archaeology is explicitly dated; settlement hiatus from one trench is not generalized to total regional abandonment. Writing is normalized Old South Arabian bn bn from GE Ṣ́ǝrḥan 1, not Geʿez or a fabricated translation.

Imported 1878 to 1900 polygon bounds 22.138 to 25.958 E, 7.551 to 11.069 N correspond to an eastern Central African region, not Rabih’s later Borno capital Dikwa. Narrative explicitly separates phases and warns geometry cannot represent his full state. No other existing Rabih/Borno card is treated as an alias.

Composite imported 1878 to 1914 record, bounding box 29.425 to 34.181 E, 8.586 to 3.711 S. Narrative expressly separates Urambo/Mirambo, Unyanyembe and Nyungu’s Ukimbu. Imported endpoint is not Mirambo’s death or a common state ending. No alias added. Ending chronology cites Shorter and Pawełczak; Unyanyembe 1893 independently checked in Gooding et al., also cited in narrative.
